passage:
I’m Deepika, and I sit behind Tushar in class, so I saw his phone all last week. He and half the boys are in a fan war against the followers of another actor. At first it was only jokes and funny edits, and Tushar laughed so hard he wheezed.
Then the comments changed. He typed something nasty under a rival fan’s photo, and the group chat filled with cheering replies. Imran, sitting beside him, did not reply at all and just kept scrolling.
Tushar looked thrilled, as if he were on a team in a real match. Later the rival fan wrote, “Why are you all so mean?” Tushar went quiet. I can’t know what he felt, but he locked his phone.

qa.q: How did the fan war begin, according to Deepika?
qa.a: It began as jokes and funny edits, and Tushar laughed so hard he wheezed.

qa.q: What might Tushar have felt when the group chat cheered his nasty line?
qa.a: He may have felt thrilled and part of a team, since he looked as if he were in a real match. The cheering rewarded him for going further.

qa.q: What could Tushar try when the banter starts to hurt someone?
qa.a: He could stop typing and picture the rival fan reading the words. Then he could decide whether the line is still a joke or has turned into cruelty.

qa.q: How might Imran, who kept scrolling, have seen the fight?
qa.a: Imran may have felt uneasy about the cruelty but did not want to break the group's mood. The passage shows only that he did not reply, so his reason is a guess.

grounding: Shows a teenage fan joining a fan war that slides from joking into cruelty, seen through an observer's account.

passage:
Monday. Sahil’s group of school friends posted jokes about a rival star’s new film, and rival fans posted jokes back. Sahil laughed at every reply and felt part of a team.
Wednesday. The jokes got sharper. Sahil posted an edited photo mocking how a rival fan looked, and the chat filled with “savage” and “more!” Chetan did not reply.
Friday. The rival fan, a girl, wrote, “I thought this was about films.” Sahil’s stomach dropped. He typed a mean answer, then deleted it. Chetan sent him a private message: “Bro, that one went too far.”
Sahil looked at the message for a long time, then took the photo down.

qa.q: What did the rival fan write on Friday?
qa.a: The rival fan wrote, “I thought this was about films.”

qa.q: Why did Sahil delete the mean answer he had typed?
qa.a: Sahil's stomach dropped when he saw that the rival fan was hurt. The cheering had made him feel like part of a team, but her message made him see a real person.

qa.q: What made Chetan's private message a good move?
qa.a: Chetan did not shame Sahil in front of the group. A short private message made it easier for Sahil to step back.

qa.q: How might the rival fan have felt seeing the edited photo and the cheering replies?
qa.a: She was likely hurt and outnumbered. Her reply, that she thought it was about films, shows she expected fun and got mockery instead.

grounding: Shows a teenager enjoying a fan war with friends as banter turns into cruelty, and then noticing the harm.

passage:
'Did you see what your Neel Roy fans posted?' Sharmila shoved her phone at Imran. 'They called Kiara's new song "funeral music".'
Imran grinned. 'Well, your side called Neel "a talking haircut". That was funny.'
'That was banter. This is war.' Sharmila's eyes were bright. 'We're trending a hashtag tonight. Everyone's in.'
'What hashtag?'
She hesitated. '#NeelFansAreUgly.'
Imran's grin faded. 'Ugly? Sharmila, my cousin's in that fan club. She's twelve.'
'It's not about her. It's about them.'
'She is them.'
Sharmila looked at the screen. Someone had already posted a photo of a girl in a Neel T-shirt with a cruel caption. Her stomach turned. 'I didn't mean like that.'
'Then don't post it,' Imran said quietly.

qa.q: What hashtag was Sharmila's side planning?
qa.a: #NeelFansAreUgly.

qa.q: What did Sharmila feel when she saw the photo of the girl in the Neel T-shirt?
qa.a: Her stomach turned; she felt uneasy and guilty, realising the 'war' had turned cruel toward real people.

qa.q: What could Sharmila do next?
qa.a: Not post the hashtag, and tell her fan group she won't join in insults about people's looks.

qa.q: How might Imran's twelve-year-old cousin feel if the hashtag trended?
qa.a: Hurt and targeted, called ugly just for loving a singer.

grounding: Teenage fans of rival singers enjoy an online war that slides from banter into cruelty toward real people.

passage: In Class 10 I was in a fan army. That's what we called ourselves: the Starlight Army, fans of the actress Mira Deshpande. Whenever someone posted a bad review of her films, we flooded their comments. It felt thrilling, like being on a team where everyone had your back. Then my classmate Sudha wrote a school-blog review saying Mira's new film was 'boring'. Our army found it. By evening there were two hundred comments on the blog, some calling Sudha names I won't repeat. I added one: a joke about her glasses. The next day Sudha didn't come to school. Our class teacher took the blog down and spoke to all of us. I'm Leela, and I left the army that week. I still feel sick about that joke.

qa.q: What did Sudha's school-blog review call the film?
qa.a: 'Boring'.

qa.q: How does Leela feel now about the joke?
qa.a: Leela still feels sick with guilt and regret about joining the cruelty.

qa.q: What could Leela do to help repair the harm?
qa.a: Apologise to Sudha directly and support the teacher in stopping the worst comments.

qa.q: What was the pile-on like for Sudha?
qa.a: Frightening and humiliating; two hundred comments and name-calling over one review kept her away from school.

grounding: A teenager in a fan army enjoys the thrill of united attacks until it turns cruel toward a classmate.

passage: School counsellor's note, Wednesday. Rukmini (Class 9) was sent to me after Zainab's mother complained. The two girls follow rival boy bands, Skyline and Nova, and their fan groups have been fighting online for weeks. It began as jokes about dance moves. Last Friday, Rukmini's group made an edited photo of Zainab with a pig's nose and shared it in three class chats. Rukmini said, 'Everyone was doing it. It felt like we were winning.' Then she cried and said she hadn't thought about Zainab seeing it. I asked her to write down what Zainab might have felt that night. She wrote half a page. I called both families today, the photo has been reported and removed, and I will meet both girls together next week if Zainab agrees.

qa.q: What did Rukmini's group add to Zainab's photo?
qa.a: A pig's nose.

qa.q: What did Rukmini mean by 'It felt like we were winning'?
qa.a: She was caught up in the thrill of the group's war, and only later felt ashamed when she thought of Zainab.

qa.q: Why did the counsellor ask Rukmini to write what Zainab might have felt?
qa.a: To help Rukmini see Zainab as a person, not 'the other side', so she understands the cruelty.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt seeing the edited photo in three class chats?
qa.a: Humiliated and hurt, mocked in front of classmates just for liking a different band.

grounding: A counsellor's note on a rival fan war between teenagers that slid from jokes into a cruel edited photo.

passage:
Saturday night.
Best night in the fan group ever, at first. The other actor's fans started it after the trailer came out, and we went to war. Forty of us, memes flying, and my edit got 2k shares. Every time someone on our side wrote "legend" under it, I felt ten feet tall. We were an army. Around eleven it changed. Someone found a rival fan's profile, a girl called Neelam from Indore, and posted her school photo with a nasty caption. People piled on. Somebody mocked her looks. I typed "lol" and then didn't send it. My stomach turned. It's just a movie. She's a kid like me. I left the chat and went and showed Mummy. She didn't shout. She sat with me while we reported the post and the account, and said leaving was the right call. I can still see that photo.
Yogesh

qa.q: How many shares did Yogesh's edit get?
qa.a: The edit got 2k shares.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when someone posted Neelam's school photo?
qa.a: At first caught up in the thrill, then sick and uneasy; the stomach turned and the "lol" never got sent.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do right once the banter turned cruel?
qa.a: Yogesh didn't join in, left the chat, and showed Mummy that same night, and together they reported the post and the account.

qa.q: What might the pile-on feel like for Neelam?
qa.a: It could be frightening and humiliating to see her school photo mocked by strangers over a movie.

grounding: Yogesh's diary shows the thrill of a fan war against a rival star's fans and the moment it slides from banter into cruelty.
